Warm-up: Seasons are the safest opinion topic there is. Take four answers and move on - the language comes later.
Vocabulary: Ask what the word feels like on your skin, not what it translates to. Humid and damp are the pair they will confuse.
The RU/KZ toggle is off on purpose.
Grammar: One rule, then the small words
The -ing form is easy. The prepositions - on, in, into, at - are what they get wrong. Drill those.
'I enjoy to swim' and 'I prefer spring than summer'.
Practice: Let them get one wrong. Seeing the reason under a wrong answer teaches more than the rule read in advance.
Students reach for love and hate. Insist on don't mind and not keen on.
The model: First for what it says, then for how it is built. Tasks 3, 4 and 5 are the second reading.
Sources are printed under the text if a student doubts them.
Listening: Three speakers, one at a time
Play each speaker separately. Do not play 2:25 in one go.
Task 4 is where the function is heard in isolation. Worth the time.
Now you: The plan is shared; the writing is individual. Do not let one student write for two.
Collect the posts. Do not correct while they write - that is the point of a model lesson.
Wrap: Frequency adverbs came back inside the seasons paragraphs.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Saying what you like — and what you don’t

One rule covers almost all of it. The trouble is the small words in front.

Read these four sentences. They all come from the recording later in this lesson.
  • I really love catching fish in the sea.
  • I’m not keen on swimming in the sea in the summer.
  • I’m really into watching ice hockey.
  • I can’t stand large crowds.
What form does the verb take after all of these?
The patterns
PatternExampleWatch out
verb + -ingI love / like / enjoy walking.the ordinary case
verb + -ing (negative feeling)I don’t mind / can’t stand waiting.same form, opposite meaning
adjective + preposition + -ingI’m keen on swimming. I’m interested in photography.the preposition forces -ing
be into + -ingI’m into watching ice hockey.informal, very common
prefer X to YI prefer spring to summer.not prefer than
+ a noun instead also correctAll of these can take a noun with no -ing at all: I can’t stand crowds. I don’t mind the cold.
Now put the six expressions in order, from loving it most down to hating it.

FORM. After love, like, enjoy, don’t mind, can’t stand use the -ing form: I enjoy walking. Never I enjoy to walk.

PREPOSITIONS FORCE IT. keen on, interested in, into, good at — after any of these small words the verb must be -ing: keen on swimming.

A NOUN IS FINE TOO. I can’t stand crowds. I don’t mind the cold. You only need -ing when the thing you like is an activity.

Not “I enjoy to swim”, not “I’m interested in photograph”, not “I prefer spring than summer”.

STRENGTH. love → really like → quite like → don’t mind → not keen on → can’t stand. Don’t mind is not enthusiasm — it means you accept it.

FORM. After love, like, enjoy, don’t mind, can’t stand the verb takes the -ing form: I enjoy walking, I can’t stand waiting. This is the single most useful thing in the lesson, because I enjoy to walk is one of the most common mistakes learners make at this level and it never stops sounding wrong. Spelling: swim → swimming (double the consonant), make → making (drop the e).

PREPOSITIONS FORCE THE -ING FORM. keen on, interested in, into, good at, tired of — whenever one of these little words comes before a verb, that verb must end in -ing. There is no exception: I’m interested in learning, never interested in learn or interested in to learn. If you can remember only one rule, remember this one, because prepositions turn up everywhere.

A NOUN WORKS JUST AS WELL. You do not always need a verb: I can’t stand crowds. I don’t mind the cold. I’m keen on photography. Use -ing only when the thing you like or dislike is an activity. If it is a thing, a place or a kind of weather, a plain noun is correct and sounds more natural.

The three mistakes to watch: “I enjoy to swim” (wrong form) · “I’m interested in photograph” (wrong word class — you need the noun photography or the -ing form) · “I prefer spring than summer” (it is prefer X to Y).

STRENGTH MATTERS AS MUCH AS FORM. love → really like → quite like → don’t mind → not keen on → can’t stand. Two of these mislead learners: don’t mind sounds positive but only means you accept something, and not keen on is a polite way of saying you dislike it. English speakers use both to avoid sounding rude.

Five real sentences from the coursebook recording.

Full grammar reference — like / love / enjoy / don’t mind / can’t stand + -ing

Form

PositiveI love cooking. · She enjoys swimming.
NegativeI don’t like getting up early. · I can’t stand waiting.
QuestionDo you like cooking? · Does he enjoy it?
Short answersYes, I do. / No, I don’t.
The scalelove > like > don’t mind > don’t like > can’t stand

Spelling and sound

-ing spelling: make → making · sit → sitting · study → studying · lie → lying.

When and why we use it

  • To say how you feel about an activity, not a thing: I love swimming.
  • Enjoy, don’t mind and can’t stand take only the -ing form.
  • Like and love can also take to + verb with almost no change in meaning: I like to read in the evening.
  • I don’t mind means ‘it is not a problem for me’ — it is not negative.

Signal words

really · quite · at all · very much

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I enjoy to read. → I enjoy reading.Enjoy is always followed by -ing.
  • I can’t stand to wait. → I can’t stand waiting.Same rule for can’t stand.
  • I am liking this song. → I like this song.Like is a state verb: no continuous form.
  • I don’t mind to help. → I don’t mind helping.Mind takes -ing.

Don’t confuse it with

I don’t mind (it’s fine) is not the same as I don’t like (it’s negative).

Stage 5 · Main input · ★ model

The model post

Read this as a writer, not just as a reader. At the end of the lesson you will write your own.

Before you read: someone from Japan is answering the question when should I come?

Which season do you think they will tell visitors to avoid? Choose one, then read and find out.

No right answer yet. This is your prediction.

When is the best time to come to Japan?

Kenji · Nagano · posted in Ask a local

Visitors always ask me this, so here is my honest answer.

Spring. I love watching the cherry trees open. In Tokyo they usually flower around 20 March and are at their best about a week later; in Sapporo you wait more than five weeks longer. It is our most pleasant season, and every park turns into a festival. But avoid the first week of May, because the whole country is on holiday. I can’t stand travelling then.

Summer. Be careful. Our rainy season runs from about 7 June to 19 July. It is damp, cloudy and very humid, and in Tokyo it rains on nearly half of those days. I don’t mind carrying an umbrella, but many visitors find it uncomfortable. From late August, about three typhoons a month come near us, often with thunder and lightning. It is hot, and it is a nasty period for a trip.

Autumn. My favourite. I prefer October to any other month. The light is beautiful and I really enjoy walking under the red leaves.

Winter. Do you like skiing? Then come. I don’t mind the cold, and the snowfall in our mountains is one of the great pleasures of living here. It’s worth the journey.

The best time to come is late October. Don’t miss it.

Sources. Cherry-blossom dates: Japan Meteorological Corporation, which forecasts about 1,000 viewing sites from somei-yoshino trees · rainy-season averages (7 June – 19 July since 1951) and rainfall probability: Japan Meteorological Agency · typhoon frequency: JMA.
